_metadata.description: Quantitative persona parameters for Chicago Racial Segregation ABM
sources: Farley et al. 1994 ASR 59(5):750-780 - showcard preference experiments
Krysan et al. 2009 AJS 115(2):527-559 - video neighborhood experiment
Card, Mas & Rothstein 2008 QJE 123(1):177-218 - tipping points
Bruch & Mare 2006 AJS 112(3):667-709 - discrete choice preference functions
Fossett 2006 J Math Sociology 30(3-4):185-273 - calibrated Schelling
Krysan & Crowder 2017 Cycle of Segregation - housing search
US Census Bureau ACS 2008-2012 5-year - Chicago income data

nh_other.label: Other (Two or more races, AIAN, NHPI)

neighborhood_composition_preferences._doc: Ideal and threshold percentages of own-group in neighborhood. Calibrated to reproduce Census 2010 dissimilarity indices: D_bw=0.825, D_hw=0.563, D_aw=0.449.
_sources: Farley et al. 1994 ASR 59(5):750-780 - showcard preference experiments
Krysan et al. 2009 AJS 115(2):527-559 - video neighborhood experiment
Bruch & Mare 2006 AJS 112(3):667-709 - discrete choice preference functions
Card, Mas & Rothstein 2008 QJE 123(1):177-218 - tipping points
Charles 2003 Annual Review of Sociology 29:167-207 - comparative racial preferences
Massey & Denton 1987 AJS 92:802-825, 1989 Social Forces 67:281-315 - Hispanic/Asian lower segregation
Iceland & Scopilliti 2008 Social Forces 87:427-451 - Asian lowest segregation among minorities
Logan & Zhang 2010 Demography 47:821-844 - Asian SES-driven residential choice
Krysan & Crowder 2017 Cycle of Segregation - differential housing search

max_outgroup_tolerance._doc: Max fraction of each outgroup before dissatisfaction sharply rises

nh_white.notes: White residents most sensitive to racial composition. Farley 1994: ~50% unwilling to enter 20% Black neighborhood. Card et al. 2008: tipping point ~5-13% Black. Bruch & Mare 2006: preference decline roughly linear with steepening above 20% Black.

nh_black.notes: Farley 1994: modal preference ~50% Black-50% White. Aversion to all-White neighborhoods due to anticipated discrimination. Krysan & Crowder 2017: social network constraints limit search to familiar areas.

hispanic.notes: D_hw=0.563 — significantly lower than Black segregation. Charles 2003: Hispanic tolerance for diverse neighborhoods much higher than Black or White. Massey & Denton 1989: Hispanic segregation driven more by economics and language than racial avoidance. Krysan & Crowder 2017: Hispanic 'gateway communities' (Pilsen, Little Village, Back of the Yards) historically function as entry points with high turnover and diversity. Iceland 2009: Hispanic suburban dispersal accelerating, reducing residential clustering. Ideal own-group lowered from 0.50→0.25 to reflect that Hispanic segregation is primarily an artifact of immigration/language concentration, not strong in-group preference.

nh_asian.notes: D_aw=0.449 — lowest segregation among minorities. Iceland & Scopilliti 2008: Asian Americans are the least segregated minority; their residential patterns are driven primarily by SES (school quality, income, safety) not racial composition. Logan & Zhang 2010: Asian residential choice is 'SES-led' — higher income Asians disperse into White-majority suburbs with good schools. Park & Iceland 2011: highest suburbanization rate, most mixed neighborhoods. Chicago-specific: outside Chinatown (Armour Square), Asians are broadly distributed in north side suburbs and university areas. Ideal own-group lowered from 0.30→0.12 to reflect that only a small fraction (first-generation Chinese) have strong enclave preferences.

nh_other.notes: Small heterogeneous group (multiracial, AIAN, NHPI). Generally tolerant of diverse environments. Parameters approximated as average of other groups with lower own-group affinity.

neighbor_preference_hierarchy._doc: Universal desirability ranking of neighbor racial groups. Scale 0-1 where 1=most desired. Based on Krysan 2009, consistent across all respondent groups.

satisfaction_function_weights._doc: Weight each factor contributes to overall neighborhood satisfaction (0-1 scale, must sum to 1.0 within each group). Calibrated so racial_composition drives White/Black segregation but NOT Hispanic/Asian over-segregation. Logan & Zhang 2010: Asian choices are SES-driven. Charles 2003: Hispanic tolerance for diversity is much higher.

nh_white._notes: White: strongest racial preference weight (Farley 1994). School and safety secondary.

nh_black._notes: Black: moderate racial preference; social network and housing cost are major factors (Krysan & Crowder 2017).

hispanic._notes: Hispanic: LOW racial composition weight — segregation driven by economics/language/social networks, not racial avoidance. Charles 2003: Hispanics show weakest racial neighborhood preferences among non-White groups. Housing cost and social network are dominant factors.

nh_asian._notes: Asian: LOWEST racial composition weight — residential choice is SES-led (Logan & Zhang 2010). School quality is dominant factor (Park & Iceland 2011). Commute also important for professional workers. Iceland & Scopilliti 2008: Asian segregation is lowest and declining.

mobility_parameters._doc: Annual mobility rates and moving decision parameters. Based on CPS mobility tables ~2010 and Krysan & Crowder 2017.

dissatisfaction_threshold._doc: Satisfaction score (0-10) below which agents actively seek to move

move_probability_function._doc: P(move) = base_rate * dissatisfaction_multiplier. When satisfaction < threshold, multiplier increases.

housing_search_parameters._doc: How agents search for new neighborhoods. Based on Krysan & Crowder 2017 Cycle of Segregation.

search_radius_hops._doc: Max graph distance (number of adjacent tracts) to search from current location or social anchor

search_bias._doc: Probability of searching in own-race-majority vs mixed vs other-race tracts. White/Black have strong own-area bias (Krysan & Crowder 2017). Hispanic/Asian search more broadly — their lower segregation reflects broader search patterns, not just weaker preferences.

social_anchor_weight._doc: How much social network location (family, friends, church) pulls search toward specific areas

archetype_dimensions._doc: Defines the archetype clustering grid for the AgentTorch-style strategy. Total archetypes = 5 races x 4 income x 3 family x 5 neighborhood = 300 maximum (many empty).

income_bracket._doc: Based on Chicago per-capita income quartiles from processed data

current_neighborhood_type.classification_rule: Dominant if single race >= 70%; asian_enclave if Asian >= 30%; else mixed

archetype_dimensions.estimated_active_archetypes: ~120-180 (many race x neighborhood combinations have zero population)

archetype_modifier_rules._doc: How archetype dimensions modify the base persona parameters

neighborhood_context_modifiers._doc: Being in a same-race dominant neighborhood reduces desire to move; mismatch increases it

exposure_indices_2010._doc: Empirical exposure indices from Chicago 2010 Census tract data (pop-weighted avg). Used as initialization targets.

holc_legacy_effect._doc: HOLC redlining grades affect neighborhood desirability as historical reputation

environmental_quality_normalization._doc: Range of tract-level attributes used to normalize environment scores to 0-1
